item.description: Beta-ecdysterone has one notable resistance-training trial and a larger preclinical literature. Here is what that evidence can—and cannot—show.

item.title: Citrulline for Strength Training: What the Pump Evidence Shows
item.description: Citrulline may help selected high-volume exercise outcomes, but pumps and acute rep changes are not proof of larger muscles or stronger 1RMs.

item.title: HMB for Strength Athletes: What the Evidence Shows
item.description: HMB may be useful in some high-stress or low-training contexts, but meta-analyses do not support routine strength or muscle gains in trained lifters.

item.title: L-Carnitine for Strength Athletes: What the Research Shows
item.description: L-carnitine has a role in fatty-acid transport, but evidence for strength and hypertrophy in healthy lifters is limited and context-dependent.

item.title: Vitamin D for Strength Athletes: Test First, Supplement Carefully
item.description: Vitamin D can matter for bone and muscle health when status is low, but there is no universal athlete target or guaranteed strength benefit from extra supplementation.

item.title: Betaine Supplementation: What the Strength Evidence Shows
item.description: Betaine is biologically plausible, but most strength and power outcomes are inconsistent. Here is how to judge the supplement without overselling it.

item.title: Vitamin D and Muscle Building: What Trials Actually Show
item.description: Vitamin D supports bone and muscle biology, but supplementation appears most useful when status is low and does not reliably add strength to already-replete athletes.

item.title: Astaxanthin for Athletes: What Exercise Research Shows
item.description: Astaxanthin changes some post-exercise biomarkers in studies, but current evidence does not establish better strength, muscle growth, or endurance performance.

item.title: BPC-157 for Injury Recovery: What the Evidence Shows
item.description: BPC-157 has extensive preclinical interest but sparse human evidence. Here is what that means for injury claims, safety, regulation, and training decisions.

item.title: Citrulline Malate: What the Pre-Workout Evidence Shows
item.description: Citrulline malate may help some exercise-performance outcomes, but the evidence is mixed and does not justify fixed promises about reps, soreness, or muscle growth.

item.title: Dileucine and Muscle Protein Synthesis: What One Trial Shows
item.description: A small human trial found dileucine increased muscle protein turnover versus leucine, but that does not yet prove more strength or muscle in training.

item.title: PQQ for Muscle Health: What Human Evidence Shows
item.description: PQQ changes some mitochondrial-related biomarkers in human studies, but evidence for strength, hypertrophy, or recovery in trained lifters is lacking.

item.title: Spermidine for Muscle Health: What Human Evidence Shows
item.description: Spermidine is linked to autophagy in laboratory research, but direct evidence for better muscle or strength in trained humans remains limited.

item.title: Supplement Stacking: What Works Together and What Is Uncertain
item.description: How to combine creatine, protein, caffeine, and other supplements without inventing synergies, ignoring interactions, or turning a simple routine into a guessing game.

item.title: Supplement Timing: Creatine, Protein, and Caffeine
item.description: Which supplements depend mostly on daily consistency, which may affect an acute workout, and how to avoid turning timing into needless complexity.

item.title: Urolithin A for Muscle Health: What Human Trials Show

item.title: Natural HGH Boosters: What Lifters Should Know
item.description: Sleep and training influence growth-hormone pulses, but supplement claims about raising HGH rarely translate into more strength or muscle.

item.title: AI Fitness Programming: Recommendations, Data, and Limits
item.description: AI workout systems can turn training history into recommendations, but useful programming still depends on data quality, transparent rules, and human judgement.

item.title: Anabolic Resistance: Protein and Muscle in Older Adults
item.description: Age can reduce the acute muscle-protein-synthesis response to feeding or exercise, but older adults can still gain muscle. Here is what protein and training evidence supports.

item.title: Ashwagandha for Lifters: What the Exercise Evidence Shows
item.description: A cautious review of ashwagandha trials in resistance training, including what may help, what remains uncertain, and the safety questions to check first.

item.title: Autoprogression: How to Choose the Next Training Load
item.description: A practical guide to using reps, RIR, RPE, and performance trends to adjust the next load—without claiming that an app can predict the perfect session.

item.title: Beta-Alanine for Strength Training: Where It Fits
item.description: Beta-alanine raises muscle carnosine, but its clearest performance evidence is for hard efforts lasting roughly one to ten minutes—not automatic strength or hypertrophy.

item.title: Blood Tests for Lifters: What They Can and Cannot Tell You
item.description: A clinician-led guide to testosterone, cortisol, CK, CRP, and other blood tests—what they measure, what they do not prove, and when testing is worth discussing.

item.title: Body Types and Training: What Somatotypes Can—and Cannot—Predict
item.description: Ectomorph, mesomorph, and endomorph labels describe appearance, but they do not prescribe your calories, exercises, or genetic ceiling.

item.title: Cluster Sets: A Way to Redistribute Rest, Not a Guaranteed Growth Upgrade
item.description: Cluster sets can preserve rep quality and reduce fatigue, but current trials do not show that they build more muscle than well-matched straight sets.

item.title: Cold-Water Immersion and Muscle Growth: Separate Soreness from Adaptation
item.description: Cold water can change soreness and perceived recovery, but repeated post-lifting immersion may not be neutral for adaptation; use it for a specific need, not as a default ritual.

item.title: How to Build Muscle: A Practical Starting Plan
item.description: A clear starting plan for muscle gain: choose productive training, eat enough protein and energy, manage fatigue, and adjust from your own record.
